item.title: The hoop2vec bracket
item.description:
The 2027 NCAA tournament will have 76 teams, up from 68, with a 12-game Opening Round before the usual round of 64. hoop2vec already has a projected bracket for it, with each team’s odds of reaching each round.

Until Selection Sunday the field is a projection. Each conference’s automatic bid goes to its tournament champion, or to its highest-rated team until that tournament is played, and at-large bids and seeds follow Power, the site’s team rating. After Selection Sunday the real bracket replaces the projection automatically.

Exact odds

Most bracket models simulate the tournament thousands of times and count how often each team wins. hoop2vec works out the odds exactly. It has a win probability for every possible game, including each team’s travel to that game’s site, so it can calculate each team’s chances round by round without any simulation noise.

Right now Illinois has a 21 percent chance to win the title. That’s the best of any team, and it still means Illinois loses somewhere along the way about four times out of five. Houston is second at 14 percent, and Connecticut is the only other team above 10 percent.

Picks

I’ve spent a lot of time over the years trying to predict upsets. One approach was to predict how many upsets would happen in a round, given the matchups, and then force that many of the most likely ones into my picks. hoop2vec doesn’t do anything like that. Its picks come straight from the probabilities.

It fills out a bracket two ways. Most likely takes the favorite in every game. Pool-optimal is built for a pool that scores rounds 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, and 32 points, so it picks the likeliest champion first and works backward from there. Right now the two brackets are close, and both expect about 88 points out of a possible 192.

Winning a pool takes more than being right. You also want to be right when the other people in your pool are wrong. hoop2vec doesn’t know what your coworkers are picking, so it can’t help with that part.

March is also just hard to predict. In 936 past tournament games, every reasonable model I tested landed within noise of the others, including a plain efficiency rating. A single tournament is 75 games, which isn’t nearly enough to tell good models apart.

item.title: hoop2vec prospects: the draft and what comes after
item.description:
I’ve always thought the eye test was worth something. Not just for seeing a player’s skills, but for seeing how competitive he is and what his drive is like. I knew Marcus Smart and Christian Braun were going to play hard at the next level. I could tell Trae Young was going to be a difficult talent to fit around, and that Andrew Wiggins didn’t have the killer instinct you’d want. That’s all fun. But for the most part, who gets drafted and who sticks in the NBA can be modeled with reasonable accuracy.

The Prospects page on hoop2vec runs two of those models on every D-I player. Right now its top prospect is Quentin Coleman, an 18-year-old freshman guard at Illinois who’s averaging 20.7 points a game. It gives him a 65 percent chance of going in the first round.

Two models

The draft model estimates the chance a player is picked in the top 5, in the lottery (the top 14), in the first round, and at all. It learned from every D-I player-season since 2008 and who actually got drafted.

The success model estimates the chance a player gets 8 or more Win Shares in his first four NBA seasons. Win Shares is a stat that splits a team’s wins among its players, and eight over four years is about what a steady rotation player gets. Players who went undrafted or never reached the NBA are in the data too, as misses.

Both models use the same inputs: age, height, class, recruiting ranking, team and conference strength, role, and about 30 stats adjusted for opponents. Age matters more than anything else. A freshman putting up good numbers at 18 is a much better bet than a senior putting up the same numbers at 23.

How well it works

I tested both models one draft at a time, training each only on earlier drafts. From 2012 through 2026, an average of 20 of the model’s top 30 players were drafted. A simple baseline using recruiting ranking, box plus/minus, and age got about 15.

NBA teams are still better at this than I am. For players who were drafted, where they were picked predicts their NBA careers better than my success model does, and adding my model to the draft slot didn’t improve on the slot alone. Teams get workouts, medical reports, and interviews. I get box scores. The model also only covers college players, so international and G League prospects aren’t on the board, and its slots run ahead of where players will really go.

Each prospect also gets comps. A separate model learns how college stats turn into NBA stats over a player’s first four seasons, then finds past college players at the same stage whose projected NBA profile is closest. Coleman’s closest comps include V.J. Edgecombe, Jeremiah Fears, and Dylan Harper, three freshman guards picked in the top seven in 2025. Some things carry over better than others. Rebounding, blocks, assists, and how many threes a player takes translate well. Shooting efficiency and overall impact translate much less.

None of this is hard to show. ESPN, KenPom, or Sports Reference could offer this kind of detail in a way that’s easy to use. They also have years of existing pages and habits to work around, and I got to start from scratch.

item.title: hoop2vec identities: how teams play
item.description:
Houston forces a turnover on about one in five possessions, takes a lot of mid-range jumpers, rebounds 40 percent of its own misses, and sends opponents to the line often. hoop2vec calls that a Mid-Range Shot-Makers offense, a Full-Court Chaos defense, and a Deep Platoon roster.

Every team gets an identity card like this one, describing how it plays separately from how good it is. The Styles tab has all the dimensions and archetypes, and which teams fit each one.

How it’s built

The cards start from play-by-play data, which logs every shot, rebound, turnover, foul, and substitution. From that I compute about 32 rates for each team, like how often it shoots in transition, where its shots come from, how many of its baskets are assisted, and how often it ends up shooting late in the shot clock. Each rate is adjusted for opponents and home court, and pulled toward average when there isn’t much data yet.

Then I take team strength out. Good teams make more shots and turn it over less, and I didn’t want a style score that was really just a quality score. What’s left goes through factor analysis, which finds groups of rates that tend to move together. Transition shots, pushing the ball after defensive rebounds, and short possessions all rise and fall together, so they become one dimension called Pace & Transition. There are six of these for offense, seven for defense, and five for the roster.

Teams also get archetypes, which are clusters of teams with similar profiles, and a team can sit between two of them. Houston is a 64 percent match for Full-Court Chaos and a 20 percent match for Conservative Pack-Line.

Each card lists strengths, vulnerabilities, and matchup notes, with the numbers behind them. Houston’s lists Run-and-Gun Bombers as both a favorable matchup and a risky one. Its defense takes away transition chances, which those teams want, and it also gives up a lot of threes, which they also want. It’s early, so most cards are marked low confidence and still lean partly on last season.

What it doesn’t do

Style barely helps predict games. Adding these dimensions to the forecasts improved log loss by about 0.001 over all games, which is tiny, and by nothing measurable in March. Almost everything a matchup tells you is already in how good the two teams are. So the forecasts leave the identities out, and the cards are there to describe teams.

item.title: hoop2vec players: value and impact
item.description:
Florida is playing without Boogie Fland, who’s out with a shoulder injury. He’d been playing about 25 minutes a game, and as long as he’s listed as out, hoop2vec takes about two points off Florida in every forecast. That adjustment comes from the Players page, which rates every D-I player.

Each player gets two numbers. Value is how many points per 100 possessions better his team is with him on the floor than it would be with an average D-I player. Impact adds playing time. It’s what he adds to his team’s rating compared with a replacement-level player, the kind of guy any team could find at the end of its bench. A great player who plays 15 minutes a game doesn’t add as much as a very good one who plays 35.

Right now the top Value belongs to Vanderbilt’s Tyler Tanner, a 6-foot junior guard, at +11.2. The top Impact belongs to Thomas Haugh, a 6-foot-9 senior at Florida who plays 33 minutes a game and is making 51 percent of his threes. So Florida is down a rotation guard, but it still has the most important player in the country.

Value starts from box plus/minus, a standard way to estimate a player’s contribution from his box score. hoop2vec adjusts each game for the strength of his team and the opponent as of that morning. Early in the season there isn’t much to go on, so the number starts from a prior built on what he did last season, the usual jump for his class, and his recruiting ranking. As minutes pile up, this season takes over. A freshman with five good games is still partly rated on his recruiting ranking, and by February he won’t be.

Injuries come from public injury reports, which hoop2vec reads every morning. A healthy player counts at 100 percent, a questionable one at 50, and a player ruled out at zero. The team ratings already reflect who’s been playing, so the adjustment only counts the difference between who’s available now and who usually plays. If a starter has missed the last three games, the ratings already know. If he’s out tonight for the first time, the forecast moves.

item.title: The hoop2vec model that was too good
item.description:
Everyone who works with data leaks it eventually. Leakage is when a model gets to see information it wouldn’t have had at the moment it’s supposed to be predicting, and it’s very easy to do by accident. When you test a basketball model on past seasons, you pretend it’s the morning of each game. The hard part is making sure the model only knows what someone could have known that morning. If anything from later sneaks in, the model looks better than it really is.

An early version of hoop2vec had a leak. In testing, it beat the betting lines on NCAA tournament games, which a model built on free public data shouldn’t be able to do. Sportsbooks have the same data and a lot more reason to get it right. That’s what sent me looking.

The leak was in a player stat that rates every player for every game, an estimate of how much he helped his team that night. To make those ratings fair, the stat adjusts for how good his team and the opponent are, and it does that using each team’s rating from the end of the season. That’s fine for looking back on a season, which is what the stat is meant for. It’s a problem for predicting one. Add up a team’s player ratings in November and you get a number that partly knows how good the team will be in March.

On its own, that one number beat the betting line in all ten seasons I checked. Once I redid the player ratings using only the team ratings from the morning of each game, the same number lost to the line in all ten. The full model got worse too. Its tournament forecasts went from beating the betting lines to trailing them slightly, which is about where an honest public-data model should be.

If you’re early in a data science career, this is the part worth taking seriously. You’ll leak data at some point. What matters is taking steps to avoid it, checking for it when results look too good, and being honest about it when it happens.

item.title: hoop2vec predictions: every game, every morning
item.description:
Duke plays at Florida on December 1. hoop2vec has Florida winning 78 to 73, with a 68 percent chance. Every D-I game gets a forecast like that, on the Games page and on each team’s page, and they update every morning.

Move the same game to a neutral floor and it’s close to a coin flip. Florida’s chance drops to 55 percent. The Matchup Lab lets you set up any game that way: pick two teams and a site, and the full model runs in your browser and shows how much each piece mattered.

How it works

The forecast blends two models. One is a neural network that takes about 40 numbers for each team, from both ratings to shooting, rebounding, turnovers, roster strength, injuries, rest, and travel. It sees both teams at once, so it can pick up on styles that match up well or badly. The other is a plain linear model built on team ratings, home court, travel, rest, and injuries. It can’t learn matchups, but it’s harder to fool. The final forecast is 70 percent network and 30 percent linear, a split I picked by testing different weights on past seasons.

The model also estimates how uncertain each game is. For Duke and Florida it’s about 12 points, meaning the final margin should land within 12 points of the prediction about two times out of three.

To test it, I had the model predict every D-I game from 2012 through 2026 as if it were the morning of the game. It could only learn from earlier seasons, and it only saw injury news that was public before tip-off. That’s about 82,000 games, and it picked the winner in 73.5 percent of them. The score I care more about is log loss, which punishes a confident wrong forecast much harder than an unsure one. On that, the blend beat both of its parts and every rating it’s built from.

Against the books

The real test is a sportsbook. ESPN carried DraftKings closing lines for about 5,500 games last season, and the lines were a little more accurate than the model, with a log loss of 0.542 against 0.547. The same has been true so far this season.

Around 2020 I was burned out from open-source work and the never-ending demands of teaching, research, and mentoring. So naturally I spent my free time trying to beat the stock market, predict elections, and model sports betting. What I found is that models are powerful and informative, but the real edge comes from data other people don’t have, or from knowing something they don’t. Public data gets you close to the market. It doesn’t get you past it.

So that’s not what hoop2vec is for. It’s for giving myself information that’s easy to digest, as accurate as I can make it, and easy to make sense of: who’s actually good, who’s overrated, which teams are worth following, and which ones would be fun to pencil in on a bracket.

item.title: hoop2vec ratings: one number for every team
item.description:
Most college basketball ratings come down to one number per team. On hoop2vec that number is called Power, and right now Illinois leads at +42.0, about five points ahead of Houston. Arkansas Pine Bluff is last at −33.4.

Power is how many points per 100 possessions a team would beat an average Division I team by on a neutral floor, so zero is average. A possession is one trip down the court, ending when the other team gets the ball, and a typical game has about 70 for each side. That makes +42 worth about 29 points against an average team in a normal game.

Counting per possession takes pace out of it. A slow team that wins 60 to 40 and a fast team that wins 90 to 70 both won by 20, but the slow team did it with fewer chances. The team pages also turn Power into odds. Illinois would beat an average team 96 percent of the time on a neutral floor, and a typical top-25 team 71 percent of the time.

Where it comes from

Underneath Power are three ratings. The first is adjusted efficiency, the approach Ken Pomeroy made famous: points scored and allowed per 100 possessions, adjusted for opponent and venue. hoop2vec recalculates it from scratch every day and gives recent games a little more weight. By that measure Illinois has the best offense in the country, scoring 131.5 points per 100 possessions against an average defense.

The second is a dynamic rating that updates after every game and keeps track of how sure it is. Early in the season it leans on last year’s team and how much of the roster came back. The third is Elo, the system chess uses, which is mostly there as a baseline.

Those three feed the game model, the same one that makes the forecasts, along with player data, injuries, and a bunch of box score stats. To get Power, I ask that model how each team would do on a neutral floor against each of the top 100 teams, then shift the scale so an average team lands at zero. Measuring against good opponents keeps a team from padding its number on bad ones. Beating the 350th-best team by 40 doesn’t say much about March.

The ratings page also has strength of schedule, which is the average Power of the teams you’ve played. Florida is 6-1 against the 12th-toughest schedule in the country. UCLA is 6-0 against the 315th. The records look about the same until you see who they came against.

It’s November, and most teams have played four to seven games, so all of this will move. Illinois’s dynamic rating comes with an uncertainty of about five points either way, which is roughly its whole lead over Houston.

item.title: Introducing hoop2vec
item.description:
hoop2vec is a men’s college basketball site I built this fall. It rates all 365 Division I teams, forecasts every game, and updates itself every morning during the season, all from free public data.

There are team and player ratings, a projected 2027 bracket, NBA draft projections, and a Matchup Lab where you can pit any two teams against each other at any site. There are also pages on how each team plays and on how the whole thing works. I’ll write about each part over the next couple of weeks.

The name is a nod to word2vec, a method that learns a list of numbers for each word based on the words around it. I liked the idea of doing that for teams and players. hoop2vec doesn’t actually use word2vec or anything like it, at least not yet. I kept the name anyway.

Why college basketball

I went to graduate school at the University of Kansas. I tutored players on the men’s and women’s basketball teams and went to a bunch of games. I live in Michigan now, and I still crave Free State Brewing Company and Burger Stand about once a week. That’s most of why I care about college basketball as much as I do. It also means my favorite team is the correct favorite team.

I’ve been building models for it on and off for about ten years, going back to a college basketball dataset I put on data.world. I’ve tried to predict upsets. I’ve tried strange hybrids of Bayesian models, latent variable models, Elo, XGBoost, and a transformer fine-tuned on press coverage. A few of them filled out my brackets. I usually compared them against KenPom, and mostly what I learned is how simple and effective KenPom is. The site still looks like it’s from the 90s, though, and I’ve always thought there was room for small innovations and features built around that approach. That’s a lot of what hoop2vec is.

How it got built

From about 2014 to 2020 I was making things all the time and sharing most of them, a lot of it on Twitter. Some of it was academic and some of it was just for fun. Then COVID hit, I had my first kid, and I changed careers. Now there are two young kids at home, and side projects pretty much stopped.

What’s different now is that I can do this kind of work from my phone. I describe what I want to Claude Code, it writes the code, and I read what it did and push back. Most of hoop2vec got built that way, a few minutes at a time.

It started as two separate projects. On the first, I described what I wanted and how I thought it should be done, then gave Claude Code license to build it and propose improvements. The second I directed much more strictly, iterating on what I thought would work. Then I merged the good ideas from both into hoop2vec, keeping whichever piece tested better where they overlapped.

I’m not very happy about working this way. I like control, and I like knowing how every piece works. I have less of that here than I’d want. But I’ve spent years building up expertise in analytics and data science, and this gives me a way to use it much faster than I could by typing everything myself. Without it, hoop2vec wouldn’t exist.
